messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Chef
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Violence: Violence, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds, Loss of Control: Lack of control
  Maladaptive Strategies: Revenge Fantasies: I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury, Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
  Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening, Hopelessness: I have no future

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi had always taken pride in his culinary skills, working his way up to become a sous chef at a trendy restaurant in his early twenties. But everything changed on a night out with friends six months ago. They had been drinking and laughing together when Kofi decided to leave early, walking home through a deserted alleyway. That's where he was grabbed by two men who dragged him into an abandoned building and assaulted him. The memory of that night still haunts Kofi in vivid detail – the feeling of being pinned down, unable to move or escape; the sounds of laughter and footsteps echoing off the walls as his attackers mocked him. But it's not just the visual memories that linger; whenever he hears car sounds, like screeching tires or revving engines, he's instantly transported back to that alleyway. The noises trigger a rush of adrenaline and a desperate urge to flee. Kofi tries to make sense of what happened by replaying the events in his head, wondering if there was something he could have done differently. He often finds himself imagining scenarios where he gets revenge on his attackers – beating them up or reporting them to the police – but these fantasies only leave him feeling more anxious and agitated. As a chef, Kofi is used to being in control of his environment, but since the assault, he's become hyper-vigilant about potential threats. He constantly scans his surroundings for signs of danger, even when working in the kitchen or walking home at night. His body monitoring has become an automatic habit; every creak of a door or sudden movement by a colleague puts him on edge. Kofi struggles to articulate what happened that night, often losing track of his thoughts mid-sentence. When he tries to explain it to friends or family members, he feels like he's reliving the trauma all over again. He's also started experiencing auditory recall – hearing sounds in his head that remind him of the assault, like muffled laughter or footsteps. At home, Kofi feels just as much on guard as he does outside. He's always checking locks and peering through windows to ensure no one is watching him. His friends have noticed a change in him too; they've commented on how jumpy and irritable he's become. Despite their efforts to reach out, Kofi has pushed them away, feeling like he's lost touch with the person he used to be. Kofi often wonders if others would have coped better in his situation – if someone else would have been able to fend off the attackers or report the incident without hesitation. This self-doubt eats away at him, fueling a deep sense of hopelessness about his future. He can't shake the feeling that he's forever changed by what happened and that no one will ever truly understand. Lately, Kofi has found it increasingly difficult to perform even simple tasks without being overwhelmed by anxiety. His work is suffering as a result – orders are getting mixed up, and colleagues have started to notice his increasing irritability. It was after a particularly rough service when he finally broke down in tears that Kofi realized he needed help. With the support of his best friend, he's now seeking therapy, hoping to break free from the cycle of fear and self-blame that's consumed him since that fateful night.
